title: Osiris: Kingship in a Funerary Hymn
subtitle: Order, loss, and return in Egyptian tradition

ani.work: Hymn to Osiris in the Papyrus of Ani
ani.author: various Egyptian authors
ani.locator: Hymn to Osiris in the Papyrus of Ani; local text normalized characters 94392-94886
ani.excerpt: Glory be to Osiris Un-Nefer, the great god who dwelleth in Abydos, king of eternity, lord of everlastingness, whose existence endureth for millions of years. Eldest son of the womb of Nut,[1] begotten by Keb,[2] the Erpat,[3] lord of the crowns of the South and North, lord of the lofty white crown, prince of gods and men: he hath received the sceptre, and the whip, and the rank of his divine fathers. Let thy heart in Semt-Ament[4] be content, for thy son Horus is established on thy throne.
ani.note: Verbatim translation excerpt; whitespace normalized. Keep the ancient text separate from Budge's editorial notes.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: The opening hymn in the Papyrus of Ani addresses Osiris as an enduring king and says Horus is established on his throne. This passage praises and invokes Osiris; it does not narrate the whole story of his death and restoration.

narrativeBlocks.title: The hymn names Osiris and Horus
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Budge translation; whitespace normalized): “Glory be to Osiris Un-Nefer, the great god who dwelleth in Abydos, king of eternity, lord of everlastingness, whose existence endureth for millions of years. Eldest son of the womb of Nut,[1] begotten by Keb,[2] the Erpat,[3] lord of the crowns of the South and North, lord of the lofty white crown, prince of gods and men: he hath received the sceptre, and the whip, and the rank of his divine fathers. Let thy heart in Semt-Ament[4] be content, for thy son Horus is established on thy throne.”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: The passage links Osiris' kingship with Horus' succession. Treat it as a funerary hymn from one manuscript, not a single canonical timeline for all Egyptian traditions.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read the evidence carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Budge's anthology translates and introduces the papyrus. Keep his edition and translation attached; distinguish the hymn's words from his notes about them.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: As you read other funerary texts, ask who is speaking, to whom, and what the text is meant to do.
